(CNN) -- Watch out! Lock up your loved ones! Another bloated, over-produced, high-concept monstrosity has escaped from the labs at Dreamworks Animation, and it's out to devour your kids. Susan, aka "Ginormica," has to save the world in "Monsters vs. Aliens." But don't be too alarmed. "Monsters vs. Aliens" is relatively harmless -- a toothless satire with a knee-jerk feminist theme and a sorry excuse for a plot. That sounds harsh, I know. Who doesn't want to see a 50-foot woman careening through San Francisco on skates that turn out to be automobiles -- the ultimate demolition roller derby? But think about that, just for a second. Roller skates work because they have fixed wheels. Try it with motorcars and you won't get very far. Is that too picky? Perhaps, but you wouldn't find Pixar playing so fast and loose with the laws of physics, and that kind of inattention to detail is typical of the lackadaisical storytelling here and in other Dreamworks animated features. (The talent pool for this one includes the directors of "Shrek 2" and "Shark Tale" and the writers of "Kung Fu Panda" and "The Rocker," incidentally.) High concepts, top-notch voice talent and scattershot pop cultural references are no compensation for a coherent script. The XXXL lady in question -- dubbed "Ginormica" by her U.S. military guards -- starts out plain and petite Susan Murphy (voiced by Reese Witherspoon), until a meteorite hits her just minutes before she's supposed to tie the knot with unctuous chauvinist Derek (Paul Rudd). Her rapid growth spurt saves her from that particular fate worse than death, even if at first glance her new roommates don't look like much of an improvement. There's Dr. Cockroach (Hugh Laurie), a mad scientist who semi-advertently mutated with a bug; B.O.B. (Seth Rogen) an amorphous blue jelly-like blob who gets on just fine without a brain; Missing Link (Will Arnett), a gung-ho amphibian who's all mouth; and a giant dust mite called Insectosaurus who isn't voiced by anyone because he doesn't have anything to say. Sci-fi fans will have fun counting off the references to myriad classics -- "Close Encounters of the Third Kind," "Invaders from Mars," "The Fly," "The Creature from the Black Lagoon," "The Blob," "Mothra" and "Attack of the 50-Foot Woman," for starters -- and noting a few clever bits and pieces (Kiefer Sutherland, as General W.R. Monger, riffs on George C. Scott in "Dr. Strangelove"). The trouble is, once the introductions are over, the filmmakers can only launch their desperately limp plot: The White House turns to these monstrous superheroes to save the planet from evil Gallaxhar (Rainn Wilson), a squidlike creature with four eyes and twice as many legs, and a one-eyed tin robot to do his dirty work for him. Ginormica gets a kick-butt finale, and is a much stronger character -- in any number of ways -- than the movie's president. (In a genuinely witty casting touch he's voiced by Stephen Colbert.) That may be good politics or at least a sound marketing decision from the studio's perspective -- it's been awhile since a family animated feature produced a genuinely strong female character (unless you count "Coraline," which was way too scary for my family) -- but Susan's self-esteem is an awfully long time coming. iReport.com: What do you think of 'Monsters vs. Aliens'? (Bizarrely -- and maybe it's just my imagination -- Gallaxhar bears a passing resemblance to President Obama. I wonder ... would that make Susan/Ginormica a surrogate for Sarah Palin or Hillary Clinton?) Visually, too, "Monsters vs Aliens" is undistinguished, although its shortcomings may be disguised if you seek out the 3-D version. Funny how 3-D movies tend to produce two-dimensional characters, with "Coraline" again the exception to the rule. Jocular and unpretentiously trashy, "Monsters vs. Aliens" should be a lot of fun -- and it is, in places. But the truth is it's as hung up on itself as Susan's preening fiance. Hand on heart, I had a better time at "Space Chimps." "Monsters vs. Aliens" runs 94 minutes and is rated PG. For Entertainment Weekly's take, click here.

(CNN) -- Beware! Shield your loved ones! Another bloated, over-produced, high-concept monstrosity has escaped the laboratories of DreamWorks Animation, and it's coming for your children. Susan, better known as "Ginormica," must save the world in "Monsters vs. Aliens." But there's no need for alarm: the film proves relatively harmless—a toothless satire built around a knee-jerk feminist theme and a threadbare plot.

That may sound harsh, I admit. Who wouldn't want to watch a fifty-foot woman careening through San Francisco on skates that transform into automobiles—the ultimate demolition roller derby? But consider it for a moment: roller skates function because their wheels are fixed in place. Attempt the same trick with cars, and you won't get very far. Is this too pedantic a complaint? Perhaps—but one would never catch Pixar playing so fast and loose with the laws of physics, and this kind of carelessness with detail typifies the lax storytelling found throughout this film and other DreamWorks animated features. (Notably, the talent behind this project includes the directors of "Shrek 2" and "Shark Tale," alongside the writers of "Kung Fu Panda" and "The Rocker.") Grand concepts, first-rate voice talent, and scattershot pop-culture references cannot compensate for the absence of a coherent script.

Our XXXL heroine—christened "Ginormica" by her U.S. military guardians—begins life as the unassuming Susan Murphy (voiced by Reese Witherspoon), until a meteorite strikes her mere minutes before her wedding to the unctuous, chauvinistic Derek (Paul Rudd). Her sudden growth spurt spares her from that particular fate worse than death, even if her new companions don't initially appear to be much of an upgrade. Among them: Dr. Cockroach (Hugh Laurie), a mad scientist who inadvertently fused with an insect; B.O.B. (Seth Rogen), an amorphous, blue, jelly-like blob who manages perfectly well without a brain; Missing Link (Will Arnett), an overzealous amphibian who is all bravado; and a colossal dust mite named Insectosaurus, who has no voice actor because he has nothing to say.

Science-fiction enthusiasts will delight in spotting nods to countless classics—"Close Encounters of the Third Kind," "Invaders from Mars," "The Fly," "Creature from the Black Lagoon," "The Blob," "Mothra," and "Attack of the 50 Foot Woman," among others—along with a handful of clever touches (Kiefer Sutherland, voicing General W.R. Monger, channels George C. Scott's performance in "Dr. Strangelove"). The trouble is that once introductions conclude, the filmmakers can only set in motion their painfully thin plot: the White House enlists these monstrous heroes to defend the planet against the villainous Gallaxhar (Rainn Wilson), a squid-like creature boasting four eyes and twice as many legs, aided by a one-eyed tin robot who handles his dirty work.

Ginormica is granted a rousing finale and emerges as a far more compelling character—in numerous respects—than the film's president (a genuinely inspired casting choice, voiced by Stephen Colbert). That may reflect sound politics, or at least savvy marketing on the studio's part—it has been some time since a family animated feature delivered a genuinely strong female lead (unless one counts "Coraline," which proved far too frightening for my household)—yet Susan's journey to self-assurance feels agonizingly protracted.

iReport.com: What do you think of "Monsters vs. Aliens"?

(Curiously—and perhaps this is merely my imagination—Gallaxhar bears a fleeting resemblance to President Obama. One wonders: might this render Susan/Ginormica a stand-in for Sarah Palin or Hillary Clinton?)

Visually, too, "Monsters vs. Aliens" fails to distinguish itself, though its shortcomings may be somewhat masked in the 3-D version. It's curious how 3-D films so often yield two-dimensional characters, with "Coraline" once again standing as the exception. Playful and unpretentiously trashy, "Monsters vs. Aliens" ought to be great fun—and in places, it is. Yet the truth remains that the film is as preoccupied with itself as Susan's preening fiancé. Hand on heart, I enjoyed "Space Chimps" more.

# Movie Review: Another Dreamworks Creature Feature Hits Theaters

(CNN) -- Parents, brace yourselves! Yet another oversized, heavily marketed animated spectacle has emerged from Dreamworks Animation's creative labs, ready to consume your children's attention. In "Monsters vs. Aliens," a character named Susan (nicknamed "Ginormica") must rescue humanity. However, there's no need for genuine concern here—this film poses little real threat, delivering a watered-down satirical take with a surface-level feminist message wrapped around a weak narrative foundation.

I recognize this assessment sounds severe. After all, who could resist watching a fifty-foot giantess zip through San Francisco streets on skates that somehow function as vehicles—essentially the greatest demolition derby ever imagined? Yet consider this logic for a moment: roller skates operate because their wheels remain fixed in position. Attempting the same mechanics with automobile wheels simply wouldn't function. This might seem like nitpicking, but Pixar productions never take such casual liberties with basic physics—and this careless approach to detail characterizes the sloppy storytelling found throughout this and other Dreamworks projects. (Worth noting: this production brought together the directing team behind "Shrek 2" and "Shark Tale," alongside writers responsible for "Kung Fu Panda" and "The Rocker.") Ambitious concepts, impressive celebrity voice casting, and rapid-fire pop culture nods simply cannot substitute for a well-constructed screenplay.

Our oversized heroine—christened "Ginormica" by military personnel guarding her—originally existed as an unremarkable, average-sized woman named Susan Murphy (voiced by Reese Witherspoon). Everything changes when a meteor strikes her mere moments before her scheduled wedding to Derek (Paul Rudd), a smug and self-important chauvinist. Her sudden transformation into a giant conveniently rescues her from this dreadful marital fate, though her new companions initially appear equally unappealing as roommates.

This monster crew includes Dr. Cockroach (Hugh Laurie), a scientist whose experiments accidentally merged him with insect DNA; B.O.B. (Seth Rogen), a shapeless blue gelatinous creature thriving despite lacking any brain function; Missing Link (Will Arnett), an overly confident amphibious being who talks big; and Insectosaurus, a massive dust mite creature who remains silent throughout since he has nothing to communicate.

Science fiction enthusiasts can entertain themselves spotting homages scattered throughout the film—nods to "Close Encounters of the Third Kind," "Invaders from Mars," "The Fly," "The Creature from the Black Lagoon," "The Blob," "Mothra," and "Attack of the 50-Foot Woman" among others. Sharp-eyed viewers will also catch clever touches, like Kiefer Sutherland's General W.R. Monger channeling George C. Scott's performance in "Dr. Strangelove."

The problem emerges once character introductions conclude—the creative team seems unable to develop anything beyond a painfully thin storyline: Washington enlists these unconventional heroes to defend Earth against the villainous Gallaxhar (Rainn Wilson), a squid-like alien sporting four eyes and eight legs, accompanied by a menacing single-eyed robotic enforcer.

Ginormica ultimately receives a satisfying action-packed conclusion, emerging as a considerably more compelling character—by multiple measures—than the film's presidential figure (cleverly voiced by Stephen Colbert, representing genuinely inspired casting). This narrative choice may reflect smart politics or savvy marketing strategy from the studio's perspective, given how rarely family animated films feature genuinely empowered female protagonists (setting aside "Coraline," which proved far too frightening for family viewing in my household)—though Susan's journey toward genuine self-confidence takes considerable time to develop.

(Strangely enough—perhaps this is merely my perception—Gallaxhar's design seems to echo President Obama's appearance somewhat. This raises an odd question: does this make Susan/Ginormica a stand-in figure for either Sarah Palin or Hillary Clinton?)

From a visual standpoint, "Monsters vs Aliens" fails to distinguish itself, though these weaknesses might be masked somewhat if viewers choose the 3-D theatrical experience. Interestingly, 3-D animated films frequently produce flat, underdeveloped characters—with "Coraline" again standing as the notable exception to this pattern.

Playful and unashamedly lowbrow, "Monsters vs. Aliens" should deliver substantial entertainment value—and occasionally it succeeds. Yet ultimately, the film seems just as self-absorbed as Susan's vain fiancé. Honestly speaking, I found "Space Chimps" more enjoyable overall.

"Monsters vs. Aliens" has a runtime of 94 minutes and carries a PG rating.

# A Toothless Satire: Reviewing "Monsters vs. Aliens"

DreamWorks Animation's big-budget production "Monsters vs. Aliens" arrives with considerable visual polish and star power, yet ultimately delivers what can only be described as a toothless satire. Beneath its glossy CGI surface lies a film burdened by a shallow, knee-jerk feminist theme and a plot so thin it struggles to sustain even its modest runtime. The film seems more interested in checking boxes of contemporary relevance than in crafting a genuinely compelling or coherent narrative.

At the center of the story is Susan Murphy, voiced by Reese Witherspoon, an ordinary woman whose life is upended on her wedding day. Struck by a mysterious meteorite mere moments before she is set to marry her chauvinistic fiancé Derek (voiced by Paul Rudd), Susan undergoes a dramatic transformation, growing into a fifty-foot giant dubbed "Ginormica." This premise, rich with potential for exploring themes of female empowerment and self-discovery, is squandered through execution that prioritizes surface-level messaging over meaningful storytelling.

One of the most glaring issues the reviewer identifies is the film's careless disregard for logical and physical consistency. This sloppiness is perhaps best exemplified in a sequence where Ginormica improbably roller-skates on car tires through the streets of San Francisco. The scene, meant to be a spectacle of action and comedy, instead highlights the screenplay's willingness to sacrifice believability for the sake of a visual gag, undermining audience investment in the world the film has constructed.

To its credit, "Monsters vs. Aliens" boasts an impressively talented voice cast bringing life to a roster of quirky, memorable characters. Hugh Laurie lends his voice to the eccentric Dr. Cockroach, Seth Rogen provides comic relief as the amorphous B.O.B., Will Arnett voices the fish-out-of-water Missing Link, and the film also features the endearing, wordless Insectosaurus. Despite these charming character designs and committed vocal performances, however, they cannot compensate for a script that feels fundamentally incoherent, jumping between plot points without the connective tissue needed to make the story feel cohesive or emotionally resonant.

Ultimately, the reviewer draws a pointed comparison between DreamWorks' approach here and the meticulous craftsmanship typically associated with Pixar. Where Pixar's films are often lauded for their disciplined attention to detail—both in narrative logic and emotional authenticity—"Monsters vs. Aliens" exemplifies a more careless, scattershot approach to filmmaking. This contrast underscores a broader critique: that spectacle and star-studded voice casts, however impressive, cannot substitute for the rigorous storytelling discipline that elevates animated films from merely entertaining to truly memorable.

# Monsters vs. Aliens: A Missed Opportunity Wrapped in Spectacle

DreamWorks Animation's "Monsters vs. Aliens" arrives with all the hallmarks of a potential animated classic: a clever premise, a stacked voice cast, and the studio's signature visual polish. Unfortunately, the film's execution reveals the cracks beneath its shiny CGI surface.

The story centers on Susan Murphy (voiced by Reese Witherspoon), an ordinary young woman whose wedding day takes a bizarre turn when a meteorite strikes her, imbuing her with the ability to grow to fifty feet tall. Dubbed "Ginormica" by the government that immediately captures her, Susan finds herself relocated to a secret facility housing other monstrous misfits: the intelligent but insect-headed Dr. Cockroach (Hugh Laurie), the gelatinous and simple-minded B.O.B. (Seth Rogen), the half-ape-half-fish hybrid The Missing Link (Will Arnett), and the massive grub-like Insectosaurus. When an alien robot sent by the tyrannical Gallaxhar (Rainn Wilson) threatens Earth, this ragtag team of monsters is recruited by the military to save the planet, since conventional forces prove useless against the extraterrestrial threat.

On paper, this setup offers rich potential: a fish-out-of-water narrative about self-acceptance, a subversive team of "freaks" turned heroes, and a chance to satirize both monster movies and alien invasion tropes simultaneously. The voice cast certainly delivers—Laurie brings wit to Dr. Cockroach, Rogen's comedic timing suits B.O.B.'s dim-witted charm, and Stephen Colbert adds sharp energy as the blustering President Hathaway.

Yet despite these strong ingredients, the film struggles to coalesce into something more than the sum of its parts. The plot feels thin, functioning more as a loose framework for action set-pieces and visual gags than a fully realized narrative. Character motivations shift conveniently to serve plot needs rather than emerging organically from established personalities, and the internal logic of the world—how the monsters' powers work, why certain rules apply inconsistently—often buckles under scrutiny. The film's satirical elements, which could have offered biting commentary on government paranoia, Cold War-era monster movies, or societal othering, instead skim the surface, delivering easy jokes without deeper insight or consistent follow-through.

This shortfall speaks to a broader pattern within DreamWorks' output during this era: a tendency to lean heavily on eye-catching 3D spectacle, celebrity voice casting, and pop-culture-savvy humor while neglecting the narrative scaffolding that gives animated films lasting resonance. "Monsters vs. Aliens" looks impressive and features talented performers clearly having fun with their roles, but the story itself never quite justifies its ambitious premise. The result is a film that entertains in isolated moments but fails to build the emotional or thematic coherence that separates truly memorable animated features from merely competent ones.

Ultimately, "Monsters vs. Aliens" stands as a case study in squandered potential—a film with all the right pieces that never quite assembles them into something greater than a serviceable, forgettable diversion.

# The Watchmaker's Lock

In a small workshop nestled at the corner of Meridian Street, an old craftsman named Elias Grant had spent forty years repairing watches. His hands, weathered and precise, could disassemble the most intricate timepieces and restore them to perfect function. But it was his latest project that had caught the attention of local news—a story that would eventually be picked up by CNN's technology desk.

Elias had partnered with his granddaughter, a computer science graduate, to create something unprecedented: a smart lock system that used a convolutional neural network (CNN) to recognize the unique wear patterns on antique watches. The idea was elegant in its simplicity. Instead of relying on traditional keys or even fingerprints, the lock would authenticate access by analyzing a watch's mechanical signature—the specific scratches, the way gears meshed, the subtle irregularities that made each timepiece as unique as a fingerprint.

"Every watch tells a story," Elias explained to the CNN reporter who had traveled to interview him. "The wear on the crown, the pattern of oxidation on the case back, even the way the second hand ticks—these are things that can't be replicated, even by the most skilled forger."

The CNN model, trained on thousands of images of watch components, learned to identify these microscopic details with startling accuracy. Users would simply hold their watch up to a small scanner embedded in the lock, and the neural network would analyze the image in milliseconds, comparing it against a stored profile.

The system garnered attention not just for its novelty, but for its philosophy. In an age of fingerprint scanners and facial recognition, Elias and his granddaughter had created something that celebrated craftsmanship and history rather than replacing it. Security experts noted that the approach was surprisingly robust—counterfeiting a watch's exact wear pattern proved nearly impossible.

By the time the CNN segment aired, Elias's small workshop had received hundreds of inquiries. What started as a grandfather-granddaughter project had become a testament to how old-world craftsmanship and cutting-edge technology could turn a simple watch into the most personal key imaginable.

# "Monsters vs. Aliens": A Derivative Disappointment That Never Escapes Pixar's Shadow

*CNN Entertainment Review*

DreamWorks Animation's "Monsters vs. Aliens" arrives in theaters with all the visual polish money can buy and about as much emotional depth as the 3D glasses you'll wear to watch it. It's a film that mistakes volume for wit and spectacle for substance—a pattern we've come to expect from a studio perpetually running in Pixar's rearview mirror.

**The Plot Holes You Could Drive a Mothership Through**

Let's start with the premise: Susan Murphy gets hit by a meteor on her wedding day and grows to 50 feets tall. Fine, we'll accept the absurdist logic of monster movies. But the film never bothers explaining how quantonium—the MacGuffin powering this entire plot—actually works, why it specifically targets Susan, or why an alien overlord named Gallaxhar needs to destroy an entire planet to retrieve a substance he could presumably just, you know, ask for.

The government's monster containment facility has apparently held creatures like B.O.B. (a mindless blob) and Dr. Cockroach for decades without anyone noticing—yet somehow Susan's transformation becomes an immediate five-alarm national security crisis. The internal logic simply doesn't hold up past the first act, assuming you're an audience member older than seven.

**Where's the Heart, DreamWorks?**

Compare this to Pixar's "Up," released the same year, which spent its opening ten minutes crafting a wordless montage so emotionally devastating that grown men wept in theaters. "Monsters vs. Aliens" spends its first ten minutes on wedding jokes and CGI meteor effects, prioritizing spectacle over story at every turn.

The film wants us to care about Susan's journey of self-acceptance, but it's so busy cramming in explosions, celebrity voice cameos, and video-game-style action sequences that the emotional beats feel perfunctory—checkboxes ticked rather than genuine character development. Pixar understands that audiences connect with vulnerability; DreamWorks seems to think audiences connect with things blowing up in three dimensions.

**The Voice Cast Deserves Better**

Reese Witherspoon, Seth Rogen, and Hugh Laurie are all talented performers essentially phoning in generic "type" voices—the everywoman, the doofus, the eccentric intellectual—archetypes so thin they could be interchanged with any other DreamWorks film without anyone noticing.

**The Verdict**

"Monsters vs. Aliens" isn't without merit—the 3D animation occasionally dazzles, and there's a kinetic energy to the action sequences that will keep young children entertained for 94 minutes. But entertained isn't the same as moved, and distracted isn't the same as delighted.

While Pixar continues to prove that animated films can tackle mortality, identity, and loss with sophistication, DreamWorks remains content to lob genre spoofs and pop culture references at the screen and hope something sticks. "Monsters vs. Aliens" is a perfectly serviceable babysitter, but it's not cinema that will be remembered—or rewatched—a decade from now.

**Rating: 2.5/5 stars** — Big monsters, bigger explosions, but a black hole where the heart should be.

# Monsters vs. Aliens: A Loving Tribute to B-Movie Sci-Fi Wrapped in Modern Animation

**DreamWorks Animation, 2009 | Directed by Rob Letterman and Conrad Vernon**

"Monsters vs. Aliens" arrives as both a crowd-pleasing family comedy and an affectionate pastiche of mid-century science fiction cinema, using state-of-the-art CGI to celebrate the genre's most enduring tropes while gently poking fun at them.

## Plot and Premise

The film follows Susan Murphy (voiced by **Reese Witherspoon**), an ordinary bride-to-be who is struck by a meteor on her wedding day and transforms into the fifty-foot-tall "Ginormica." Captured by the government, she's placed alongside a menagerie of similarly afflicted "monsters": the arrogant, gelatinous B.O.B. (**Seth Rogen**), the half-man/half-cockroach scientist Dr. Cockroach (**Hugh Laurie**), the missing link The Missing Link (**Will Arnett**), and the massive larva Insectosaurus. When an alien named Gallaxhar (**Rainn Wilson**) invades Earth seeking the same alien compound that empowered Susan, this ragtag team of misfits becomes humanity's unlikely last line of defense, led by General W.R. Monger (**Kiefer Sutherland**), with the hapless President Hathaway played by **Stephen Colbert**.

## Cinematic Lineage

Part of the film's charm lies in its clear reverence for classic science fiction cinema. The premise of Susan's transformation directly recalls **"The Amazing Colossal Man" (1957)** and **"Attack of the 50 Foot Woman" (1958)**, right down to her tattered wedding dress evoking the latter's iconic poster imagery. Dr. Cockroach's man-insect hybrid nods to **"The Fly" (1958)**, while the Missing Link is a clear riff on the Gill-man from **"Creature from the Black Lagoon" (1954)**.

The alien invasion narrative borrows liberally from **"The Day the Earth Stood Still" (1951)**, particularly in its themes of humanity confronting a technologically superior force, while Gallaxhar's cloning army and menacing presence echo **"Invasion of the Body Snatchers" (1956)**. The government's secret monster containment facility plays like a wink to **Area 51** mythology and films such as **"The Blob" (1958)**, where authorities scramble to hide inexplicable threats from the public.

Even the film's black-and-white newsreel-style prologue plays homage to 1950s creature features, immediately signaling the film's genre awareness to attentive viewers.

## Voice Performances

Witherspoon brings surprising emotional depth to Susan's journey from insecure fiancée to self-assured hero, while Rogen's B.O.B. provides consistent comic relief with his blissfully dim-witted charm. Laurie's clipped, dignified delivery as Dr. Cockroach adds sophistication to an otherwise absurd character, and Arnett's swaggering machismo as Link satirizes the leading-man archetype of the era's monster films. Wilson's Gallaxhar strikes an effective balance between menace and camp, embodying the theatrical villainy of vintage sci-fi antagonists.

## Verdict

While "Monsters vs. Aliens" doesn't reach the emotional sophistication of DreamWorks' "How to Train Your Dragon" (released the following year), it succeeds as a visually inventive, genuinely funny homage to a beloved film era. Its 3D animation—groundbreaking for its time—complements the larger-than-life spectacle inherent to its source material. For genre enthusiasts, the film functions almost as a scavenger hunt of references; for younger audiences, it's simply an entertaining monster mash. This dual appeal, characteristic of the best family animation, makes "Monsters vs. Aliens" a worthy, if not essential, entry in the genre-parody tradition.

**Rating: 3.5/5 stars**

# Monsters vs. Aliens: Big on Spectacle, Short on Substance

DreamWorks' 2009 animated romp "Monsters vs. Aliens" arrives with the kind of visual bombast we've come to expect from the studio, but beneath its 3D-ready explosions and alien invasions lies a script that feels more like a collection of set pieces than a cohesive story.

**A Plot That Doesn't Hold Together**

The premise—a woman struck by a meteor grows to fifty feet tall on her wedding day and joins a team of government-quarantined monsters to fight an alien invasion—is admittedly a fun hook. But the film never quite figures out what to do with it beyond the initial setup. Character motivations shift conveniently to serve the next action sequence, and the emotional beats (particularly Susan's arc of self-acceptance) feel rushed and undercooked, as if the filmmakers assumed the giant robots and goo monsters would distract us from noticing.

**Physics? What Physics?**

For a movie ostensibly about scale and size, "Monsters vs. Aliens" plays remarkably fast and loose with basic physics. Susan's fifty-foot frame changes weight, density, and proportional strength depending on whatever the scene requires—she can toppler buildings in one moment and be gently cradled in another. The alien technology operates on dream logic rather than any consistent internal rules. This isn't necessarily a dealbreaker for a family cartoon, but the inconsistency becomes distracting precisely because the film seems to want credit for its "science-based" premise.

**The Pop Culture Grab Bag**

Where the film does succeed is in its shameless, gleeful pilfering from decades of sci-fi and monster movie history. References to "The Blob," "Mothra," "E.T.," and classic Cold War-era creature features are sprinkled throughout with genuine affection. These nods provide some of the film's biggest laughs and suggest a filmmaking team that loves the genre—even if they couldn't quite translate that love into a tighter narrative.

**The Feminist Angle: A Pale Shadow of Coraline**

The film wants credit for its ostensibly feminist message: a bride abandoned by her shallow fiancé finds empowerment through monstrous transformation and found family. It's a nice idea in theory. But stack this against the same year's "Coraline"—a film that explored female agency, autonomy, and the seductive dangers of "perfect" alternate lives with genuine psychological depth—and "Monsters vs. Aliens" looks thin by comparison. Coraline's heroine earns her independence through courage and cunning in a story that trusts its audience with ambiguity and darkness. Susan's empowerment, by contrast, is largely something that *happens to her* (via meteor strike) rather than something she claws her way toward, and the film's climax resolves her arc more through spectacle than earned character growth.

**Final Verdict**

"Monsters vs. Aliens" is diverting enough as a loud, colorful spectacle for younger viewers, and monster-movie enthusiasts will appreciate its referential winks. But adults hoping for the emotional and thematic sophistication of Laika's contemporaneous masterpiece will find themselves wanting. It's a film more interested in being big than being good.

**Rating: 2.5/5 stars**

# 'Monsters vs. Aliens': A Colorful Romp That Sneaks in Some Sly Political Satire

**By CNN Entertainment Staff (Style Parody)**

There's something delightfully absurd about watching Stephen Colbert voice the President of the United States in an animated film about a woman who grows to 49 feet, six inches after being struck by a meteor on her wedding day. But "Monsters vs. Aliens," the latest 3D spectacle from DreamWorks Animation, wears its absurdity like a badge of honor—and mostly earns the right to do so.

## The Premise: Big Hair, Bigger Problems

Susan Murphy (voiced with likable everywoman charm by Reese Witherspoon) is a Modesto, California bride-to-be whose life takes a literal growth spurt on what should be the happiest day of her life. Rechristened "Ginormica" by the government, she's whisked away to a secret facility where she meets a menagerie of misfit monsters: the gelatinous B.O.B. (Seth Rogen, having an absolute blast), the erudite cockroach-human hybrid Dr. Cockroach (Hugh Laurie), the missing link fish-man (Will Arnett, dripping with himbo energy), and the massive insect Insectosaurus.

When an alien named Gallaxhar (Rainn Wilson) arrives seeking the mysterious quantonium that caused Susan's transformation, these government-quarantined outcasts become Earth's last line of defense.

## Colbert Steals Every Scene He's In

Let's address the giant, blue-suited elephant in the room: Stephen Colbert's Commander-in-Chief is a gift. Playing the President as a blustery, image-obsessed showman who's more concerned with optics than actual crisis management, Colbert brings his "Colbert Report" persona's satirical edge to the material without ever breaking the film's family-friendly stride.

There's a moment where the President attempts to communicate with the approaching alien threat by playing a keyboard rendition of "Close Encounters"—and then, when that fails, immediately pivots to blasting the aliens with military hardware while grinning for the cameras. It's a sly wink at every real-world leader who's ever prioritized a photo-op over a coherent policy. One can't help but think of actual White House press briefings where bravado substitutes for substance, or state visits that are more theater than diplomacy.

Colbert's President also has zero qualms about locking away American "monsters" indefinitely without trial or explanation—Susan and her fellow creatures have been held in secret government custody for decades, some since the 1950s—which lands with an extra satirical punch given post-9/11 anxieties about detention, surveillance, and who gets labeled a "threat" to national security. The film doesn't dwell on this too heavily (it's still selling toys and popcorn, after all), but the DNA of political satire is unmistakably there under the goo and slime.

## The Verdict: Visually Dazzling, Comedically Uneven

Directors Rob Letterman and Conrad Vernon clearly have affection for 1950s creature-features, and the film's best moments—Ginormica's size-shifting rampages through military installations, the beautifully rendered alien mothership—use 3D technology in genuinely inventive ways rather than just lobbing objects at the audience.

Where the film stumbles is in its uneven comedic rhythm. Rogen's B.O.B. gets the biggest laughs (his blissful ignorance about basically everything is a highlight), but some subplots—particularly Susan's arc with her narcissistic ex-fiancé—feel like padding between the genuinely inspired set pieces.

Still, "Monsters vs. Aliens" earns its stripes as smarter-than-average family entertainment, buoyed considerably by a voice cast that's clearly having fun subverting expectations. Colbert, in particular, proves that sometimes the best political commentary comes wrapped in eye-popping 3D and a giant blue guy.

**Rating: 3 out of 5 stars**
